books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Mississippi, Declaration of the Immediate Causes of Secession (January 9, 1861)

stimulus.source_note: Mississippi, A Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of the State of Mississippi from the Federal Union, January 9, 1861. Public domain. Wording verified against the Mississippi Department of Archives and History text (mshistory.mdah.ms.gov) and Wikisource. Passages appear in this order; '. . .' marks omitted text.
stimulus.text: . . . Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery—the greatest material interest of the world. Its labor supplies the product which constitutes by far the largest and most important portions of the commerce of the earth. . . . That blow has been long aimed at the institution, and was at the point of reaching its consummation. There was no choice left us but submission to the mandates of abolition, or a dissolution of the Union, whose principles had been subverted to work out our ruin. . . . We must either submit to degradation, and to the loss of property worth four billions of money, or we must secede from the Union framed by our fathers to secure this as well as every other species of property.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: According to the declaration, Mississippi faced which choice?

options.text: Joining the Union or joining Britain
options.misconception: The declaration weighs submission against secession, not an alliance with Britain.

options.text: Submission to abolition or dissolution of the Union
Freeing its slaves or selling them abroad
options.misconception: The declaration never considers freeing or selling slaves; it defends keeping them.

options.text: Paying four billion dollars or going to war
options.misconception: The four billion dollars is the value of the property at risk, not a price Mississippi could pay.

rationales.A: The declaration weighs submission against secession, not an alliance with Britain.
rationales.B: The declaration states the choice plainly: “submission to the mandates of abolition, or a dissolution of the Union.”
rationales.C: The declaration never considers freeing or selling slaves; it defends keeping them.
rationales.D: The four billion dollars is the value of the property at risk, not a price Mississippi could pay.
rationales.general:
1. The declaration frames the moment as a fork with two roads.
2. One road is submission, the other is leaving the Union.
3. Background: Mississippi's convention had already voted 84 to 15 to secede when it issued this declaration.
4. The “choice” is really a justification for a decision already made.
Remember: when a document says “we had no choice,” check whether the choice was real or a reason written after the fact.
